title: Theory of algorithms for unconstrained optimization
contribution: Single-author Acta Numerica survey that judges the theory of unconstrained optimization by whether it explains the methods as implemented in practice and whether it can tell efficient from inefficient methods, synthesizing Zoutendijk/Dennis-Moré principles, CG, BFGS/Broyden-class (trace-determinant self-correction, DFP's weakness), SR1 and large-scale methods, and ending with numbered open questions.
problem_entry: A user's question from a lecture: for the methods that deserve to be in a subroutine library, what is known about each as implemented in practice, and can theory tell efficient from inefficient methods (pp. 1-2); unconstrained line-search methods only, noise and rounding set aside (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Four-way classification of convergence results (global, local, rate, global efficiency; p. 2); a few principles (Wolfe, Zoutendijk, Dennis-Moré; pp. 4-7) carry most analysis; global convergence alone is a weak target, so angle tests are rejected (p. 7).
assumptions: Smooth f, gradient available, bounded below, Lipschitz gradient near the level set (pp. 4-5); strong Wolfe for CG (p. 11); strong convexity for BFGS/Broyden theory (p. 18); restrictive assumptions of global-efficiency studies and of Powell's unit-step 2-D analysis flagged (pp. 2, 8, 24).
proof_devices: Zoutendijk condition proved in full from Wolfe + Lipschitz gradient (p. 5) and its use for lim and lim inf results (p. 6)
Dennis-Moré characterization of superlinear convergence; unit trial step (p. 7)
Kantorovich inequality for steepest descent on quadratics; Nemirovsky-Yudin lower bound (pp. 8-9)
Al-Baali induction for Fletcher-Reeves sufficient descent (pp. 11-12)
tightness counterexample just past |beta_k| <= beta^FR (Gilbert-Nocedal, p. 12); Powell's Polak-Ribière cycling example (p. 13)
Property (*) and a class theorem for methods with beta_k >= 0 (p. 14)
trace and determinant relations for BFGS self-correction (pp. 18-19); Broyden-class trace relation comparing 1/cos and 1/cos^2 terms to explain DFP (p. 20)
cos theta_j bounded below for at least a fraction p of indices; potential psi(B) = tr(B) - ln det(B) (p. 21)
Powell's two-variable quadratic recurrences: DFP of order lambda vs BFGS of order log lambda iterations (pp. 23-24)
Khalfan-Byrd-Schnabel n-step q-quadratic SR1 rate (p. 29)
experiments: No new experiments; small diagnostic observations (FR tiny steps on the minimal surface problem, p. 12; CONMIN restarting every iteration, p. 15) and the Byrd-Nocedal-Yuan two-variable BFGS/DFP test matching Powell's prediction (p. 24).
positioning: Continues Powell, Dennis-Moré, Zoutendijk/Wolfe (pp. 5, 7, 17); places his group's results in that line (pp. 12-14, 17, 21, 25-26, 30-31); complexity school presented neutrally but Nesterov's optimal method judged unlikely to be practical, untested (p. 15); reports the SR1 reversal and conflicting SR1 evidence without arbitrating (pp. 27-28).
writing: First person and evaluative ('In my view', pp. 2, 10, 15); question-led sections (pp. 14, 24); numbered Open Questions I and II (pp. 17, 21-22); one full proof, the rest labelled non-rigorous heuristics (pp. 5, 19).
limits_future: Excludes rounding errors/noise, global optimization, nonlinear equations, least squares, trust-region theory (pp. 2-3, 31-32); open: comprehensive CG theory (p. 10), DFP on convex problems (p. 17), BFGS on non-convex problems and a line search bounding |y|^2/y's (p. 22), why L-BFGS is as fast as BFGS and which pairs to keep (p. 31), line search vs trust region (p. 32).

method_links.note: 'as implemented in practice' test (p. 1), efficient-vs-inefficient test (p. 2), steepest-descent argument against settling for global convergence (p. 7), family-wide trace analysis singling out DFP (pp. 17-20) and BFGS/DFP efficiency gap (pp. 23-24); open questions numbered (pp. 17, 21-22). Fills in the thin SKILL.md anatomy of this paper.

Received safeguard (angle tests) rejected by argument and by what the best codes do, not by a new experiment (p. 7); SR1 reversal reported from others' studies (p. 27); restarts 'controversial', judged with his own observation (p. 15).

Partitioned quasi-Newton for partially separable problems a major advance (pp. 29-30); L-BFGS competitive only when element functions involve more than a few variables (p. 30); CG preferred for very large problems with cheap functions (p. 10).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Isolate the property that makes Polak-Ribière good (Property (*): a tiny step away from the solution forces a small beta) and prove convergence for every method that has it.
Asks whether practical line searches would accept the counterexample's steps and whether the failure has ever been observed (PR cycling; DFP never observed to fail).

transferable: List the few methods that deserve to be in a subroutine library, with their codes, and review only what is known about each as implemented (pp. 1-3).
Classify each convergence result as global, local, rate or global efficiency and say which class is missing (p. 2).
Explain why one family member fails by comparing how each potential-function term scales in the bad regime (cos theta small); the term that vanishes at that parameter is the mechanism (pp. 18-20).
Test a tightness claim with a counterexample just past the bound (p. 12).
Before calling a method unsafe because of a counterexample, check whether practical line searches would accept its steps (p. 13).
Confirm a worst-case prediction on the smallest nearly-quadratic problem the analysis covers (p. 24).
coauthors: none (single-authored); thanks M. Lalee, C. Hartung, P. Lu (p. 32)

quotes.text: We have learned that it is preferable not to interfere with the BFGS method and to let the matrices … evolve freely, because convergence is usually obtained and the rate is superlinear
Ironically, our many theoretical studies of variable metric methods have not resulted in the discovery of new methods, but have mainly served to explain phenomena observed in practice

title: Representations of quasi-Newton matrices and their use in limited memory methods
contribution: Derives compact outer-product representations of BFGS (inverse and direct), SR1 and Broyden matrices from a product-of-projections lemma, so that limited memory matrices support the sparse, projected and direct-matrix operations of constrained methods at cost proportional to nonzeros or free variables, with parity to the two-loop recursion on unconstrained problems.
problem_entry: Limited memory methods work unconstrained, but constrained methods need projections onto active subspaces and the direct matrix B_k; the two-loop recursion ignores sparsity (H e_i as costly as H g) and has no direct-B analogue (pp. 2, 4).
key_idea: Product of BFGS projections = I - Y R^{-1} S^T (p. 5) gives H_k = H_0 + [S, H_0 Y] (2k x 2k middle) [..]^T and B_k = B_0 - [B_0 S, Y] M^{-1} [..]^T (pp. 6-8); same matrices, new representation; with scalar H_0, store S, Y and small m x m matrices (pp. 9-11); extends to SR1 (p. 21) and Broyden (pp. 23-25).
assumptions: s_i'y_i > 0 and a positive definite start for BFGS (pp. 6-7); only well-defined denominators for SR1 (p. 21); nonzero s_i and a nonsingular start for Broyden (pp. 23, 25); scalar initial matrix for efficiency (p. 10); constant m (p. 9).
proof_devices: induction for the product-of-projections lemma with the bordered triangular R (p. 5)
split H_k = M_k + N_k, each part by induction (pp. 6-7)
Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury from inverse to direct form (pp. 7-8), and for the SR1 and Broyden inverses (pp. 22, 25)
block reordering so only a positive definite m x m Cholesky factorization is needed; positive definiteness by contradiction via triangular R (p. 9)
itemized multiplication counts per algorithm step (pp. 11-20)
two-loop recursion related to the compact form and to the adjoint / reverse-mode differentiation of g -> g'Hg/2 (p. 19)
exact equivalence conditions with multiple secant updates (Y'S diagonal for BFGS; symmetric for SR1) (pp. 26-28)
experiments: none (operation counts instead: parity with the two-loop recursion on the unconstrained step, pp. 12-13; cost proportional to nonzeros or free variables, pp. 15, 18; cheaper than the straightforward approach, pp. 19-20)
positioning: Keeps the Nocedal/Matthies-Strang two-loop recursion as equally efficient unconstrained and preferable for non-scalar H_0 (pp. 13, 18-19); credits Walker (p. 5); contrasts with the Mahidhara-Lasdon straightforward approach (pp. 19-20) and with multiple secant updates, judged not advantageous for optimization and not clear cut for equations (pp. 26-28).
writing: Theorem-proof plus algorithm boxes with per-step cost (pp. 12-13, 16-17); modest hedges ('We believe', p. 3; 'as far as we know', p. 13; 'we know of no procedure', p. 19); motivation before formulas (pp. 2-4).
limits_future: No numerical tests; limited memory SR1 algorithms not detailed (p. 23); SR1 skip test expensive, triangular-factorization test suggested (p. 23); limited memory methods for nonlinear equations worth considering (p. 29); users named: the bound-constrained algorithm (pp. 16-17) and reduced-Hessian SQP (p. 25).

method_links.note: BFGS/L-BFGS matrix kept unchanged; only its representation, the component that fails in the constrained setting (p. 4), is replaced, with unconstrained cost kept equal (p. 13); no noise estimate or recovery path.

Structure exploited inside the generic method's linear algebra (sparse constraint gradients, unit-vector bounds; cost proportional to nonzeros or free variables), not by choosing a structure-exploiting method.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Linear-algebra paper that makes a known matrix usable in new settings, explicitly aimed at limited memory use; users named are the bound-constrained algorithm (S003) and reduced-Hessian SQP.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: operation counts as the evaluation protocol
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Per-step multiplication counts against each named alternative, with parity on the incumbent's home problem.

transferable: Turn a product of rank-one projections into I - Y R^{-1} S^T by induction to get a compact outer-product form (p. 5).
Reorder an indefinite block middle matrix so only a positive definite m x m Cholesky factorization is needed (p. 9).
Store S'g and Y'g from the previous iteration so the small matrices update in O(m^2) (pp. 11-12).
Show parity with the incumbent on its home problem before claiming gains elsewhere (pp. 13, 15, 18).
Compare two update formulas by finding the exact condition under which they coincide (pp. 26-28).
coauthors: Richard H. Byrd, Robert B. Schnabel (Colorado); thanks Peihuang Lu (p. 29)

quotes.text: This is true even if limited memory approximations are used, unless special care is taken in their representation and manipulation
We believe that these new compact representations of quasi-Newton matrices are of interest in their own right, but in this paper we focus on their use in limited memory methods

title: A limited memory algorithm for bound constrained optimization
contribution: L-BFGS-B: a gradient-projection / subspace-minimization algorithm with limited memory BFGS matrices in compact form, whose generalized Cauchy point and subspace step cost O(n) per iteration, benchmarked on CUTE bound-constrained problems against LANCELOT's SBMIN.
problem_entry: Large bound-constrained problems with only gradients, no Hessian or structure, storage linear in n (p. 2); enters the gradient-projection framework of Conn-Gould-Toint and Moré-Toraldo but with line searches and, mainly, L-BFGS matrices (p. 3).
key_idea: Generalized Cauchy point on the projected steepest descent path, then subspace minimization over the free variables with truncation, then a line search (pp. 3-4); the compact form B = theta I - W M W' lets each breakpoint after the first cost O(m^2) via W'd and W'z (pp. 5, 8-9); three subspace options because the best is problem dependent (p. 11); skip pairs failing s'y > eps|y|^2 without dropping the oldest (p. 6).
assumptions: Smooth f, gradient only, simple bounds, large n (p. 2); B_k positive definite gives descent (p. 4); no convergence analysis or zigzagging study, expected to carry over, trouble expected in degenerate cases (pp. 4, 15).
proof_devices: descent of d_k from the model decrease at the Cauchy point (p. 4)
heapsort of breakpoints and piecewise-quadratic f', f'' updates in O(m^2) per segment via auxiliary vectors p = W'd, c = W'z (pp. 7-9)
Algorithm CP cost: linear in n plus O(m^2) per segment plus n log n (pp. 9-10)
Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury for the reduced inverse (p. 12)
saving Y'ZZ'Y, S'ZZ'Y, S'ZZ'S across iterations and Y'ZZ'Y = Y'Y - Y'AA'Y (p. 13)
identity between the primal and dual middle matrices bringing their costs together (pp. 17-18)
experiments: L-BFGS-B (primal, dual, CG; several m) vs LANCELOT SBMIN (BFGS, SR1, exact Hessian) at default settings on CUTE bound-constrained problems with discards stated; same projected-gradient stopping test; nfg/nf and time, two failure codes (pp. 18-19); table entries illegible in the text layer; stated results: more evaluations than LANCELOT-SR1, often less time on large problems, CG least effective (p. 23); backtracking-line-search regression found by comparison with unconstrained L-BFGS (pp. 18-19).
positioning: Extends L-BFGS to bounds with similar demands (p. 4); differs from Conn-Gould-Toint and Moré-Toraldo by line search and L-BFGS (p. 3); LANCELOT used only as a benchmark, ranking disclaimed, codes assigned to different problem classes (p. 23); revises S019's view that backtracking suits constrained problems (S019 p. 8 vs p. 19).
writing: Procedural with operation counts at every step (pp. 9-10, 13-17); candid hedges where evidence is weak ('seems problem dependent', p. 11; 'To our surprise', 'not clear to us', p. 23); two-sided closing verdict tied to problem features (p. 23).
limits_future: No convergence analysis (p. 4); CG option least effective; inaccurate final location not understood and under investigation; not competitive in evaluations with exact Hessians or exploitable structure (p. 23).

method_links.note: Non-noise case: L-BFGS kept; components that break under bounds replaced one at a time (curvature-condition skip without dropping the oldest pair, p. 6; backtracking replaced by Moré-Thuente with the step capped at the nearest bound, pp. 18-19); failure isolated by comparison with the unconstrained predecessor (p. 19).

Undecided subspace-minimization choice ('seems problem dependent') built in three variants and benchmarked, later exposed as the isbmin option (S005 p. 5); unexplained failures recorded as under investigation.
States its own method is less likely to be competitive with exact Hessians or exploitable structure; assigns LANCELOT to partially separable problems.

Stopping test aligned (p. 18), rival in three Hessian options (p. 19), losses printed and ranking disclaimed (p. 23); but rival only at defaults with no option search (p. 23) while own side shown in several variants and memory sizes (pp. 21-22): an early, weaker form of the 2003 protocol.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Early bound-constrained version run against unconstrained L-BFGS on unconstrained problems; the gap located the backtracking-line-search regression.
Algorithm built on the S014 compact form; code described in the report that is S005.

transferable: Carry expensive inner products along a piecewise search with a few small auxiliary vectors so each breakpoint after the first costs O(m^2) (pp. 8-9).
Maintain positive definiteness under constraints by skipping pairs that fail s'y > eps|y|^2, without deleting the oldest pair (p. 6).
Cap the line search's maximum step at the nearest bound so a Wolfe line search works inside a box (pp. 18-19).
Use the unconstrained predecessor as a control on unconstrained problems to locate a regression (p. 19).
Report CPU time only where problems are large enough for it to be meaningful; count evaluations everywhere (p. 23).
coauthors: Richard H. Byrd (Colorado), Peihuang Lu, Ciyou Zhu (Northwestern)

quotes.text: In contrast, when using the new line search, the update is very rarely skipped in our tests, and the performance of the code was markedly better
The tests described here are not intended to establish the superiority of LANCELOT or of the new limited memory algorithm

title: Algorithm 778: L-BFGS-B: Fortran subroutines for large-scale bound-constrained optimization
contribution: The released Fortran 77 L-BFGS-B package: reverse-communication interface, documented parameters (memory m, factr, subspace method isbmin), graded drivers, restart-and-exit robustness devices and a unified primal/dual subspace step, benchmarked on CUTE bound-constrained and unconstrained problems against LANCELOT's SR1 and exact-Hessian options.
problem_entry: Users need a limited memory code for bounds: L-BFGS-B is the only limited memory quasi-Newton code handling bounds, and nonlinear CG has not been extended to bounds (p. 2).
key_idea: Package the S003 algorithm behind reverse communication with task strings (pp. 3-4); expose the undecided subspace method as isbmin (p. 5); unify the primal and dual subspace computations through one block matrix so their performance is similar (p. 8); add restart and exit devices (pp. 6-7).
assumptions: User supplies f and g, no Hessian or structure (pp. 2-3); recommended small m range (p. 3); machine precision used only in the factr test and the BFGS skipping test (p. 7); invariant to scalar multiples of variables and objective except the first step and the factr test, not to linear transformations (p. 7).
proof_devices: restart along steepest descent after line-search failure, loss of positive definiteness or a non-descent direction, then a named abnormal exit (pp. 6-7)
skipped-update counter exposed in isave (p. 7)
primal/dual subspace matrices written as the inverse of one block matrix, factorized by Cholesky of submatrices (p. 8)
experiments: CUTE bound-constrained and unconstrained problems above a size threshold; LANCELOT SR1 and exact Hessian at default options; one projected-gradient stopping test for all runs (p. 8); nfg/nf and CPU; C/F markers grading non-converged runs against LANCELOT-SR1's f (pp. 10-11); stated results: competitive, more evaluations, comparable CPU with great variability, larger m more reliable but slower, primal and dual similar, CG slower (pp. 8-9); table entries illegible in the text layer.
positioning: Extension of L-BFGS (Harwell VA15) performing similarly on unconstrained problems, could supersede it except for extra storage (pp. 1-2); the only limited memory code for bounds (p. 2); follows MINPACK ideas and style (p. 16).
writing: User-manual voice with direct recommendations ('We recommend that every user of LBFGSB read this driver', p. 6; m range, p. 3; factr values, p. 4); numbered advantages and numbered drawbacks before the parameter list (pp. 2-3).
limits_future: Drawbacks: not rapidly convergent, may miss high accuracy on ill-conditioned problems, cannot use structure (p. 3); scale dependence of the factr test and of the first step (pp. 6-7); inability to reduce the projected gradient despite a good f 'deserves further study' (p. 9).

method_links.note: Subspace-minimization choice left open in S003 exposed as the isbmin parameter with a default; driver4 runs all three options on CUTE; an unexplained behaviour recorded as an open question.
Recovery-and-exit-flag step only: discard the memory and restart along steepest descent, then a named abnormal exit; no explicit estimate drives the repair.
Own code's drawback (iii): cannot use problem structure; recommended for Hessians that are not sparse or hard to compute.
One projected-gradient stopping test for every code and run; rival options declared as defaults.

Runs missing the stopping test but matching LANCELOT-SR1's f are marked C and not counted as failures (p. 9), unlike Method 1 step 4 (any test miss or limit counts as a failure); the marking is transparent but the accounting favours the authors' code.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Parity with L-BFGS on unconstrained problems claimed, and unconstrained CUTE problems shipped in the test driver.

transferable: Use reverse communication (a task string the caller switches on) so users control evaluations, stopping and timing (pp. 3-4, 6).
Ship graded drivers: minimal default, termination/output, CPU-time-limited, and a full test-and-profile driver over the benchmark set (pp. 5-6).
On line-search failure or loss of positive definiteness, discard the memory and restart along steepest descent once, then fail with a named message (p. 7).
List every place where machine precision and scaling enter the code (p. 7).
Grade non-converged runs against the rival's objective value with explicit table markers (pp. 10-11), while still counting them as failures.
coauthors: Ciyou Zhu, Richard H. Byrd (Colorado), Peihuang Lu; thanks B. Averick and J. Moré (p. 16)

quotes.text: We recommend that every user of L-BFGS-B read this driver
We do not interpret these as failures of the algorithm, but feel that this property of L-BFGS deserves further study
